extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, creative writers, and literary-minded readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing extended lyric/meditative poems: choosing a unifying subject, working from observation, and shaping coherent connections and reflections across parts. Also practical/political advice for authors about audience and livelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject should supply natural connection and unity to the poem
rubrics_metrics.description: “I sought for a subject, that should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society, yet supply in itself a natural connection to the parts, and unity to the whole.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a central, concrete subject whose inherent progression or structure ties the poem’s parts together (Coleridge’s example: tracing a stream from source to sea). The subject should create organic links between descriptive passages, incidents, and reflective passages so the whole reads as a coherent unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid awkward connections and abrupt, arbitrary transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: “I had considered it as a defect in the admirable poem of THE TASK, that the subject, which gives the title to the work, was not... and that, throughout the poem, the connections are frequently awkward, and the transitions abrupt and arbitrary.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat disjointed shifts and sudden topic-jumps as a defect. Work to smooth transitions and ensure each section follows logically or thematically from the previous to preserve flow and reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose from direct observation and make ‘studies’ in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: “My walks therefore were almost daily on the top of Quantock, and among its sloping coombes. With my pencil and memorandum-book in my hand, I was making studies, as the artists call them, and often moulding my thoughts into verse, with the objects and imagery immediately before my senses.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-hand observation, on-location sketches, and note-taking to generate concrete imagery and immediate sensory detail. Grounding verse in perceptual experience helps vivid description and authentic reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose subjects that allow equal room for description, incident, and impassioned reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: “a subject, that should give equal room and freedom for description, incident, and impassioned reflections on men, nature, and society”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning an extended poem, prefer subjects broad and flexible enough to sustain multiple modes (scenic description, narrative incident, moral or emotional reflection) without forcing awkward insertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base argument and writing on principles for enduring influence
rubrics_metrics.description: “He referred habitually to principles. He was a scientific statesman; and therefore a seer. For every principle contains in itself the germs of a prophecy; and, as the prophetic power is the essential privilege of science, so the fulfilment of its oracles supplies the outward... test of its claim to the title.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounding writing (especially political or argumentative prose) in clear, articulated principles rather than ephemeral appeals or ad-hoc rhetoric gives it a durability and intellectual weight that outlasts topical fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience expectations; avoid gratuitous or misapplied offence
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the second number an essay against fast days, with a most censurable application of a text from Isaiah for its motto, lost me near five hundred of my subscribers at one blow. In the two following numbers I made enemies of all my Jacobin and democratic patrons...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that shocking or ill-judged uses of sacred texts, or unexpected political targets, can alienate readers and damage circulation. Match tone and targets to the audience you wish to retain, or accept the consequences of deliberate provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expectation: literature may not reliably sustain your livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: “I saw plainly, that literature was not a profession, by which I could expect to live; for I could not disguise from myself... they were not of the sort that could enable me to become a popular writer...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan financially and practically: do not assume literary talent alone will guarantee stable income. Seek patrons, supplementary work, or realistic expectations about commercial viability.
